zones.label: Bank
zones.tooltip: Every chip you may buy. A stack says how many are left; when stacks run dry the ante grows.

zones.label: Gem pile
zones.tooltip: The gems that will end you. Ten or more at the end of your own turn and you lose.

zones.label: Bag
zones.tooltip: Your draw pile. When it runs out mid-draw the discard goes back in and is shaken.

phases.label: Play gems for money, then buy

cards.story: A gem pile reached ten at the end of its owner's turn, and that is the game. Whoever kept theirs lower wins.

cards.tooltip: Finish your action phase and go on to buying. Any actions you have left are lost.
End your turn. You must have bought at least one chip — a Wound is free, and that is the point.
Worth 1. Play it in your buy phase for 1 gem power, or let it sit in a gem pile counting against whoever owns it.
Worth 2. Play it in your buy phase for 2 gem power, or let it sit in a gem pile counting against whoever owns it.
Worth 3. Play it in your buy phase for 3 gem power, or let it sit in a gem pile counting against whoever owns it.
Worth 4. Play it in your buy phase for 4 gem power, or let it sit in a gem pile counting against whoever owns it.
Merge two gems in your own pile into one, if they total 4 or less. Costs you a gem power, and gives you back the action you spent.
Break one gem in your own pile and send that many 1-gems across the table. A 3-gem becomes three 1-gems in their pile.
As a Crash Gem, but up to two of your gems at once.
This chip does nothing. It is free, and it is the only thing you can always afford: you must buy something every turn, and this is what is left when nothing else is in reach.
Put a gem from your hand into your own gem pile — which is the wrong direction — and take a bigger one plus three gem power for the trouble.
Each opponent gains a wound. (Its reaction half needs playing out of turn, which the engine does not allow yet.)
Draw three chips.
Four actions, and a wound to pay for them.
Ante a 1-gem into each opposing gem pile, and keep your action.
Trash a gem out of your hand and take four actions for it.
Two actions.
An action, a buy, a gem power and a chip — one of each of the four things a chip can give you.
Keep your action and draw two chips.
Put a 1-gem from your hand into your own gem pile, and it pays for itself: four chips and your action back.

+1 blue action. Each opponent gains a wound or discards two wounds. Here they gain one: choosing for them is the opponent's decision, and there is no way to ask yet.
Ongoing: negate a gem sent to you, then discard this chip. Reactions are not built yet, so laying it out does nothing but say you have it.
+1 blue action. Ongoing: nobody may combine without discarding a Puzzle chip first. The tax is not built; the action it gives back is.
Ante a 1-gem into your own pile, then take two actions and a chip for it.
Trash a wound out of your hand, and it turns into an action and a gem in every opposing pile.
A Double Crash Gem that costs you two wounds. Its reaction half needs playing out of turn, which is not built.
Ongoing: ante a gem one higher than usual, your crashes cannot be reacted to, and you cannot buy purples. The bigger ante is built; the other two clauses need reactions, which are not.
Reaction: when an opponent buys a 4-cost chip or more, trade a chip out of your hand for a better one. Reactions are not built yet.
Trash a chip out of your hand and take a 2-gem from the bank straight into it. Character chips cannot be trashed.
Choose a non-Puzzle chip in your hand or discard, play it twice, trash it, then end your action phase. Playing a chip twice is not built; the extra actions are.
An action, a buy and a chip.
Two actions and a chip.
Main: two chips. Reaction: play this as a Crash Gem to counter gems sent to you — the reaction needs playing out of turn, which is not built.
Trash a non-purple chip from your hand then gain a chip costing exactly 2 more. Comparing two chips' prices is not built, so this trashes and gives the action back.
Choose one: an action and a buy, or two gem power, or two chips.
Main: a chip and a buy. Reaction: reflect any gems sent to a player back to the bank — the reaction needs playing out of turn, which is not built.
Trash a gem out of your hand and take one worth a point more straight back into it.
Combine a 1-gem out of the bank with a gem already in your pile — which makes your pile heavier, and is the point: bigger gems crash harder.
A chip. Printed: opponents reveal their hands, trash their largest gem, then gain that many 1-gems — reading somebody else's hand is not built.
Trash up to two chips out of your hand. Character chips cannot be trashed.
Your opponent chooses which of the two you get: an action and a chip, or two gem power and a buy. Nothing makes them press the button — at one screen, hand it over.
Trash this chip and take another whole turn after this one.
A chip, and a 1-gem out of your pile and into theirs.
Any different two of: an action, a buy, a gem power, a chip.
Printed: exchange a chip in your hand with a purple from your bag. Searching a shaken bag is not built, so this gives the action back and nothing else.
Two chips, then put up to two out of your hand back on the bag. Which order they go back in is not yours to say here.
Take the top chip of your discard pile back into your hand. Printed, you may choose which — a pile is reached from the top, so this takes the last one you threw away.
Three chips and an action — but only while your own gem pile is at ten or more, which is to say only while you are already losing.
Ongoing: a chip at the end of any turn you bought a Puzzle chip. The condition is not built; laying it out draws you the chip once.
Reveal two chips at random from a chosen opponent's hand and take what they turn out to be worth. Reading somebody else's hand is not built.

cards.tooltip: Defensive disruption: wounds that clog an opponent's bag, and a ward that taxes the whole table.
Rushdown: burn your own wounds for tempo, ante gems at the other side, and finish with an uncounterable double crash.
An economy engine: trash the chips you have outgrown and buy bigger gems into your hand.
Speed: more actions, more buys, more chips, every turn.
A gambler happiest near the edge — the fuller your gem pile, the more you draw.
A generalist who takes whatever the turn needs, and answers a crash with a crash.
Stone: turn small gems into big ones and hand the incoming ones straight back.
A talker: thin your own deck, make the other player answer questions, and take what falls out.
A painter of options — every chip is a choice, and one of them is another whole turn.
Time: put the chips you want back where you will draw them, and pull the ones you need out of the past.
